review_note: Keep the short ladder slides, practical turns and research-dispute sequence. Align the claims with the lecture; remove invented classroom reactions and assertions that ordinary friendship obeys the course’s model.

edits.before: - Two openings, both real. Give them both before any theory.
edits.after: - Give both opening scenarios before the theory. They are examples, not reported cases.
edits.reason: Do not present invented examples as actual documented events.

edits.before: Three really good conversations with someone from your lab. And yet it isn't a friendship, and you can't tell what's missing.
edits.after: Three really good conversations with someone from your lab. And yet it doesn't feel like a friendship, and you can't tell what's missing.
edits.reason: Keep the scenario without adjudicating whether a relationship qualifies as friendship.

edits.before: - The finding that matters needs no number: the protocol expects hours before depth.
edits.after: - The abstract gives no timetable for an individual friendship. Keep the association separate from the course's depth model.
edits.reason: Do not infer a universal sequence or threshold from the association with time.

edits.before:
Three great conversations are three hours, not a friendship yet.

That isn't a verdict on the conversations. It's the clock.

<MarginNote label="Capacity planning">No way to buy it in one large conversation.</MarginNote>
edits.after:
Three good conversations can leave you wanting another.

Make room for one.

<MarginNote label="Capacity planning">A good conversation is an opening.</MarginNote>
edits.reason: Keep a short practical pause slide without inventing the conversations’ duration or a friendship threshold.

edits.before:
Not intimacy. **Opportunity.**

Hours are when the steps can happen. A friendship needs both: the time, *and* somebody stepping during it.

Three hours at level 1 is three hours. It is not three steps.

```notes
- This is the synthesis of Hall and the rate limit, and it answers the first opening properly.
edits.after:
More time together gives you **another chance to talk**.

The depth model asks a separate question: did either person offer a more personal turn?

```notes
- Use the two questions to explore the first scenario, not to diagnose why a friendship has not formed.
edits.reason: Treat the clock and depth model as questions rather than a complete mechanism of friendship.

edits.before: - The third is the easiest to miss. Receiving a disclosure well builds closeness on their side. Listening is a move, not a pause between moves.
edits.after: - In the third effect, the listener is the person someone has disclosed to. Listening is a move, not a pause between moves.
edits.reason: Keep the useful distinction without an unsupported claim about what readers usually miss.

edits.before: - This is Collins & Miller's third effect run as an experiment instead of meta-analysed.
edits.after: - This asks a related question: how do the assigned listener and discloser roles affect liking?
edits.reason: Do not equate the comparison between assigned roles with the third meta-analytic association.

edits.before: <MarginNote label="Handshake, again">One-sided exchange, asymmetric result. Both sides step, and it resolves.</MarginNote>
edits.after: <MarginNote label="Handshake, again">In this task, swapping roles removed the difference.</MarginNote>
edits.reason: Keep the finding specific to the task rather than a guarantee about any interaction.

edits.before:
- Read it as a protocol result. A one-sided exchange doesn't fail -- it leaves two people feeling differently about the same conversation.
- What fixes it isn't saying more or less. It is taking the other turn. That is the evidence under the rule two slides from now.
edits.after:
- After both people had listened and disclosed, the difference between assigned roles disappeared.
- This prompts attention to both sides of an exchange. It does not validate the course's five levels or its plus-or-minus-one window.
edits.reason: Preserve the result and its relevance without presenting it as proof of the invented rule.

edits.before: - Say this every time. By week 9 they should expect the caveat slide, and notice when a source doesn't get one.
edits.after: - Keep these limits attached when applying the finding to the classroom exercise.
edits.reason: Keep the teaching cue without narrating the course’s success at training its audience.

edits.before:
- Worth dwelling on. Wanting it more doesn't work, and having things in common doesn't do it either. The structure does.
- Which is good news for anyone who has been told to just relax and be themselves.
edits.after: - No significant difference in these experiments is not evidence that goals or shared attitudes never matter. Keep the result within the procedure tested.
edits.reason: Do not turn null results in a particular design into universal claims about closeness.

edits.before: - The 45 minutes worked because both people had signed up to a procedure. A café queue has no procedure.
edits.after: - The study tested an agreed procedure. It did not test an uninvited deep disclosure in a café queue.
edits.reason: Keep the context distinction without claiming to know which feature caused the result.

edits.before: The levels below are **not** from the literature. Nothing retrievable supports a five-level scale.
edits.after: The levels below are **the course's model**, not a scale validated by the cited studies.
edits.reason: State the known evidence boundary rather than claiming no supporting literature is retrievable anywhere.

edits.before: - Say this before the table, every time. The moment a student cites the depth scale as a finding, this course has failed at the thing it teaches.
edits.after: - Name the scale's status before showing the table: a model to test, not a research finding.
edits.reason: Keep the source distinction without another performance judgement about the course.

edits.before: - Now go back to both openings. The queue went 0 to 3 in one turn with no step in between. The three conversations stayed at 1, and nobody stepped.
edits.after: - Return to the examples. The queue suggests a 0-to-3 jump. For the three conversations, ask whether either person offered a more personal turn; the opening did not tell us.
edits.reason: Do not invent the contents of the first scenario to make it fit the model.

edits.before: ## Two problems, one diagnosis
edits.after: ## Try the model on the openings
edits.reason: The model offers questions, not a diagnosis of the relationships.

edits.before:
**The three good conversations:** level 1, three times. **Nobody stepped.**

```notes
- Same rule, two failure modes: too far in one step, and no steps at all. Most people have only noticed the first one.
edits.after:
**The three good conversations:** did either person offer anything beyond level 1?

```notes
- Ask what else you would need to know before explaining either exchange.
edits.reason: Let the example remain an open question instead of prescribing a result and claiming what most students notice.

edits.before: ## You've gone past the limit
edits.after: ## Possible signs of a limit
edits.reason: The working list is an interpretation to test, not a certain diagnosis from any one signal.

edits.before:
Nobody tells you. That's the problem --- the protocol has no error message for depth, only the four signals on the last slide.

So the repair has to be **self-initiated**, which week 5 already told you is the preferred kind.
edits.after:
The other person may not say directly that the topic is too personal.

If you notice a possible signal, you can **initiate the repair** yourself.
edits.reason: Keep the usable repair option without claiming nobody gives direct feedback or that only four signals exist.

edits.before: - Ask first: has anyone said the right-sized thing and had it land like nothing? Then name the method: an event-contingent diary. Then point out that this is exactly what their Field Journal is, and that they have been running a 1998 psychology method since week 2.
edits.after: - Name the method: an event-contingent diary. Their Field Journal can borrow immediate note-taking without recording every interaction as the study did.
edits.reason: Connect the methods without overstating equivalence between the journal and the research protocol.

edits.before:
Same subject. One rung higher. No extra privacy spent.

```notes
- This is the cheapest escalation step in the course, and it is additive -- nothing in the left column was wrong.
- Worth saying plainly to the half of the room who have been told they give people information and not much else: the fix is one clause, not a personality.
edits.after:
Same subject, with what it means to the speaker.

That feeling may itself be private.

```notes
- The extra clause is optional. Practise adding it when you want to share the feeling, not because the facts-only version was wrong.
edits.reason: Keep the usable example while respecting the privacy cost of emotional disclosure and removing an invented history for half the room.

edits.before: - This is the whole course arriving from the research side instead of the satirical one.
edits.after: - Keep the attribution to the abstract clear.
edits.reason: Let the result stand without announcing that it vindicates the course.

edits.before: - The last two minutes are the real finding: sentences with no feeling in them are hard to follow up, which is the previous slide from the other direction.
edits.after: - Let the group identify which sentences were harder to follow up and why. Do not prescribe a finding about sentences without emotion.
edits.reason: The activity should discover its own results; factual sentences may also invite useful follow-ups.

edits.before: - Three weeks of vocabulary in one slide: ledger, hold token, rate limit. Point that out; it is the course demonstrating its own thesis.
edits.after: - Connect the hold token to week 4: it explains a pause without requiring the disclosure itself.
edits.reason: Preserve the useful cross-week connection without congratulating the course for demonstrating its thesis.
